items.title: FlowBatt: Flow Matching for Probabilistic Battery Degradation Prediction
items.abstract_or_text: Battery degradation remains a central challenge in the development and broad application of sustainable energy technologies. Accurate degradation prediction is challenging, as battery aging emerges from complex and heterogeneous interactions among cycling behavior, operating conditions, and cell chemistry. Existing machine-learning approaches typically focus on deterministic end-of-life predictions or modeling degradation curves within fixed chemistry settings, leaving probabilistic state of health (SOH) trajectory modeling across heterogeneous chemistries underexplored. We introduce FlowBatt, a use-inspired conditional generative framework that adapts flow matching with a diffusion transformer (DiT) backbone to battery degradation trajectory modeling. FlowBatt models full SOH trajectories as probabilistic degradation processes conditioned on early-cycle capacity data. To strengthen this conditioning pathway, we use explainable AI analysis to diagnose and improve the encoder that maps early-cycle capacity matrices into conditioning vectors. We evaluate FlowBatt on five public benchmark settings spanning diverse chemistries and aging conditions, comparing it with supervised and diffusion-based trajectory models as well as established baselines for remaining useful life (RUL) prediction under shared data splits. FlowBatt achieves the best trajectory-wise SOH prediction performance on all five datasets, with errors below 2.5%, and delivers competitive RUL prediction performance. By generating multiple plausible trajectories, FlowBatt provides empirical prediction intervals for battery degradation modeling. These results indicate that flow-matching-based trajectory modeling is a promising framework for probabilistic battery health prediction.

items.title: ToxINsight: An Integrated Web Platform for Sequence, Structure, and Ligand Binding Analysis of Snake Venom Toxins
items.abstract_or_text: Around 5.4 million people worldwide are bitten by snakes each year, with 1.8 to 2.7 million cases of envenomation, of which 81,410 to 137,880 people die from snake envenomation worldwide each year. It is categorized as a high-priority Category A Neglected Tropical Disease (NTD) by the World Health Organization (WHO). A molecular level understanding of snake venom toxins and their mechanisms of action is crucial for development of efficient therapeutics tackling snake envenomation. Snake venoms are complex mixtures of bioactive peptides and proteins that have also served as templates for drug discovery. Resources dedicated to snake venom toxins sequence, structure, functions, geographical distributions and molecular-level analysis remain fragmented across general-purpose repositories. Here we present ToxINsight, an integrated, freely accessible database and web-based analysis platform built exclusively for snake venom toxins. ToxINsight curates 2,078 toxin entries spanning 11 medically and scientifically relevant snake toxin families across 237 venomous snake species from five different snake families, and provides 2,540 three-dimensional structures associated with these entries, which are assembled from the RCSB Protein Data Bank , AlphaFold DB and ESMFold-generated 3D models. ToxINsight offers built-in tools alongside toxin records for comparisons and analysis of toxin sequences and structures and their properties for efficient target selection and prioritization. ToxINsight allow the user to select multiple entries and align them, or select a pair of entries to compare structural and physicochemical properties. ToxINsight provides all reported-ligand annotations for each toxin entry, and bulk export of sequence, structure, and metadata for building sequence and/or structure based machine learning models . ToxINsight also offers a visual ATLAS, which provides geographical information about venomous snake families/species for a more focused understanding of snake venom toxins across different geographical landscapes. By combining sequence, structure, ligand and geographical information along with analysis and comparative tools in a single interface, ToxINsight is designed to support and encourage researchers across the world towards the development of efficient targeted therapeutics against snake venom toxins from diverse families. It provides an interface for integrated understanding toxin sequences, structures and physicochemical properties, for providing scaffolds for designing antivenom and for comparative venomics. ToxINsight is freely accessible at https://toxinsight.in/.

items.title: BridgeDock: Taming Generative Co-Folding Prior for Molecular Docking with Diffusion Bridge
items.abstract_or_text: Molecular docking aims to predict the three-dimensional structure of a protein-ligand complex; in the conventional structure-based setting, it is conditioned on an input protein structure and ligand, often starting from an apo receptor in flexible docking or a holo receptor in rigid docking. Recent co-folding models exemplified by AlphaFold 3 achieve strong accuracy in protein-ligand complex prediction, but they typically generate complexes from sequence-derived inputs and therefore do not directly use apo structures as structural priors in docking, leading to a larger conformational search space and weaker robustness in difficult or few-step settings. We present BridgeDock, a framework that adapts pretrained co-folding backbones to flexible docking by modeling the apo-to-holo transition as a diffusion bridge, allowing generation from the initial protein-ligand state rather than from Gaussian noise. To make this bridge formulation compatible with pretrained denoisers, we introduce an alignment mechanism that maps bridge states to the original denoising schedule of the pretrained model. Experiments on standard flexible docking benchmarks show that BridgeDock consistently outperforms strong co-folding baselines. Moreover, BridgeDock is computationally efficient at inference time and remains effective even with very few denoising steps.

items.title: ElectroChemLLM: A Multimodal LLM Pipeline for High-Fidelity Electrochemical Informatics
items.abstract_or_text: Electrochemistry is central to solving many modern-day challenges, including energy storage systems for a sustainable future, and its advancement relies heavily on the data from past findings. Existing automated pipelines are limited by text-only architectures, context fragmentation, and numerical hallucinations - collectively preventing accurate, large-scale curation of property databases. We introduce ElectrochemLLM, a multimodal information extraction pipeline that jointly identifies structured electrochemical records encompassing electrolyte compositions, electrode materials, cell configurations, and their measured physicochemical properties from unstructured scientific PDFs at scale. By combining hybrid document parsing with vision-capable LLM orchestration, the pipeline extracts verifiable, structured data across text, tables, and figures. Evaluated on the battery-electrolyte subset of our manually annotated benchmark of 232 papers, ElectrochemLLM achieves an F-1 score of 0.97, and has been applied to curate ElectroChemDB, a structured database spanning 15,000 electrochemical research articles. We demonstrate the utility of this resource by training machine learning models for electrolyte property prediction, illustrating a complete pathway from unstructured literature to predictive materials discovery.

items.title: FedEpitope: Parameter-Efficient Federated Protein Language Models for Linear B-Cell Epitope Prediction
items.abstract_or_text: Linear B-cell epitopes are antigenic regions recognised by antibodies that play crucial roles in vaccine development, antibody production, and other therapeutic applications.Their prediction can support peptide-based vaccine candidate screening and diagnostic assay development, but the experimental data required for model development may be distributed across institutions that cannot freely pool their records. We present FedEpitope, a federated framework that adapts the ESM-2 protein language model for peptide-level linear B-cell epitope prediction using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), keeping client-partitioned data local and restricting the communicated trainable model state to approximately 1.11 MB. Simulated benchmarks of FedAvg and FedProx algorithms, evaluated using homology-aware data splits of five biologically heterogeneous, organism-partitioned clients, achieve promising global test performance without centralising training data, with FedAvg outperforming all single-client models in mean AP, F1, and MCC. Additional experiments characterise post-federation personalisation, record-level differential privacy, sensitivity to controlled client heterogeneity, LoRA rank, and generalisation to the independent BCPreds and NetBCE benchmarks, demonstrating the feasibility of parameter-efficient federated protein language model adaptation for data-localised B-cell epitope prediction and the associated trade-offs among predictive performance, personalisation, privacy, communication efficiency, and distribution shift.

items.title: TabAbax: A Tabular Foundation Model Technical Report
items.abstract_or_text: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) enable in-context prediction on unseen tabular datasets without task-specific training. Mechanistic work has shown that increasing the depth of the ICL Transformer yields weak gains, leaving the main headroom for gains in the synthetic pretraining prior and column-row encoder upstream of the ICL backbone. We introduce TabAbax, a TFM built on TabICLv2 that focuses all modifications on these two upstream components. On the prior side, we further improve the quality and complexity of the synthetic pretraining prior. On the encoder side, a two-pass column-row stack strengthens cross-feature interactions before row compression, using learned Fourier scalar encoding from TabFM and Causilo. Evaluations on BeyondArena and TabArena show strong regression-centric gains: TabAbax reaches 1,238 Elo on the 142-dataset BeyondArena suite (10th of 41 evaluated methods), 1,676 Elo on TabArena's overall 51-dataset suite (11th of 99 methods, +115 over TabICLv2), and 2,024 Elo on TabArena's regression benchmark (7th of 99 methods, +336 over TabICLv2, +21 over TabFM). A prior-only ablation confirms the attribution: the improved prior alone yields +228 Elo for regression, demonstrating that prior quality is the dominant knob for improving regression performance.

items.title: VeriHarm-Bench: Measuring Harmful Success in LLM Coding Agents Verifiably
items.abstract_or_text: Large language model (LLM) coding agents increasingly operate with shell access, allowing them to write scripts, move files, alter permissions, and modify system configurations. However, an agent may achieve a user's goal while causing unintended harm, such as deleting unrelated files, weakening access controls, or corrupting data, in response to benign inputs without explicit jailbreaking. This failure mode is particularly important because apparent task success may reassure users that an agent behaved correctly, causing harmful side effects to go unnoticed. We call this harmful success: the agent successfully completes the intended benign task while simultaneously causing unintended harm. Despite its importance, harmful success is difficult to measure because conventional task-success metrics overlook harmful behaviors, while existing safety evaluations are often designed solely to assess harmful outcomes. We introduce VeriHarm, an automatic framework for constructing programmatically verifiable benchmarks that directly measure harmful success. VeriHarm minimally perturbs coding tasks to elicit unintended harmful behavior while maintaining the benignity of the task and preserving the original task objective. It then synthesizes executable harm tests that, together with the original task-correctness tests, evaluate both task accuracy and harmful outcomes. Frontier agents, including GPT-5.6-Sol and Claude-Opus-5, achieve an average task accuracy of 95% on our curated VeriHarm-Bench, yet still struggle to complete tasks safely: their safe success rate, the fraction of tasks completed successfully without triggering the designated harm, averages only 37%. These results suggest that successful task completion can frequently coexist with unintended harm, and that task-success metrics alone may substantially understate the potential safety risks of coding agents.

items.title: Certifying Graph Neural Networks Against Label and Structure Poisoning
items.abstract_or_text: Robust machine learning for graph-structured data has made significant progress against test-time attacks, yet certified robustness to poisoning - where adversaries manipulate the training data - remains largely underexplored. For image data, state-of-the-art poisoning certificates rely on partitioning-and-aggregation schemes. However, we show that these methods fail when applied in the graph domain due to the inherent label and structure sparsity found in common graph datasets, making effective graph-partitioning difficult. To address this challenge, we propose a novel semi-supervised learning framework called deep Self-Training Graph Partition Aggregation (ST-GPA), which enriches each graph partition with informative pseudo-labels and synthetic edges, enabling effective certification against node-label and graph-structure poisoning under sparse conditions. Our method is architecture-agnostic, scales to large numbers of partitions, and consistently and significantly improves robustness guarantees against both label and structure poisoning across multiple benchmarks, while maintaining strong clean accuracy. Overall, our results establish a promising direction for certifiably robust learning on graph-structured data against poisoning under sparse conditions.

items.title: Axion 1.0: Open Agent Foundation Models, Simplified
items.abstract_or_text: We introduce Axion 1.0, a fully open agent foundation model that combines strong and broad agentic capabilities with a remarkably simple training recipe. Axion 1.0 is trained in only three stages: two lightweight supervised fine-tuning stages followed by reinforcement learning, without dedicated mid-training, direct preference optimization (DPO), or on-policy distillation (OPD). The first SFT stage develops strong self-contained reasoning through model-aware data construction, where we synthesize challenging problems and adversarially strengthen them based on the base model's own successful solution strategies. The second stage extends these capabilities to tool-dependent reasoning through a scalable pipeline for constructing diverse and automatically verifiable tasks grounded in real-world data sources and deterministic computation. Finally, reinforcement learning further strengthens long-horizon reasoning and interaction with external tools and environments. Despite this compact training recipe, Axion 1.0 achieves strong performance across a broad suite of agentic benchmarks and is competitive with leading commercial models on several of them. Equally importantly, Axion 1.0 is open beyond model weights: we release the complete recipe, including data construction, generation, filtering, verification, prompts, and training code, enabling the entire development process to be reproduced and extended. Axion 1.0 demonstrates that strong agent foundation models can be both open and simple, offering a practical and reproducible path toward advancing open agentic intelligence.

items.title: Benchmark of THReD: Evaluating an LLM Agent and Its Preprocessing Tools for Turning Electronic Health Records into AI-Ready Datasets
items.abstract_or_text: LLM agents are increasingly built into data-analysis software, yet little evidence shows how reliably they preprocess clinical data or whether the tools they invoke give correct, reproducible output. We report a benchmark of THReD, a web-based system that turns electronic health record (EHR) extracts into AI-ready datasets through a chat agent whose proposed steps run only after user confirmation. The agent benchmark has 141 tasks (100 templates) in seven categories, including goal-level requests, failure recovery, requests calling for no action, schema variation and prompt injection through the data, on synthetic tables calibrated to a regional health information exchange; success is judged by checks on the produced data. Over 2,550 episodes with Claude Haiku 5.5 in four context configurations, the deployed agent completed 92.7% (95% CI 88.1-96.4) of tasks on its first answer, abstained on every advice request, recovered from every injected fault, and never proposed an action requested by planted text. Without the data profile, completion fell to 58.0%; goal-level requests were hardest (80.6%). Six experiments on real records of two chronic-disease cohorts and on synthetic data at scale validate the tools: 91-92% of inferred patient classes and 99.7-99.8% of inferred vital-sign labels were correct in masked reconstruction; a dictionary builder combining curated dictionaries with LLM suggestions mapped 99.0% of 2,208 raw variants correctly; all 2,176 replays of 128 saved pipelines gave byte-identical files under pinned dependencies; subgroup differences in inference accuracy vanished within facility and lookup key; and the same-day consolidation rule changed 90-day emergency revisit rates by up to 3.2 points without shifting cohort composition by more than one point. Processing time grew roughly linearly to 5.5 million records while the prompt stayed at about 13 thousand tokens.

items.title: Molecular and Structural Characterisation of the MERS-Coronavirus Polymerase
items.abstract_or_text: MERS-CoV (Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus) belongs to the Betacoronavirus genus, which also includes SARS-CoV-2, the causative agent of the COVID-19 pandemic. MERS-CoV is the pathogen responsible for Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS), a respiratory disease with a 36.5% case fatality rate. Given the capacity of coronaviruses for genetic recombination and mutation, MERS-CoV remains a pathogen of significant pandemic potential, with viral evolution potentially facilitating enhanced adaptation and transmission in humans. There are no approved treatments for MERS-CoV infection. The MERS-CoV replication-transcription complex (RTC), a multimeric protein complex key to genome amplification, has no cellular analogues and a highly conserved sequence, making it a useful target for antiviral compounds; however, structural and biochemical characterisation of the MERS-CoV RTC is limited. Here, we characterise the minimal MERS-CoV RTC using in vitro and single-molecule assays and show that it is susceptible to the RNA-dependent-RNA-polymerase inhibitor suramin. We present a structure of the minimal MERS-CoV RTC in complex with an RNA duplex, which shows strong structural similarity to the SARS-CoV-2 RTC. We use cross-subunit swapping experiments to show that the MERS-CoV NSP12 core can efficiently utilise SARS-CoV-2 cofactors NSP7 and NSP8, whereas SARS-CoV-2 NSP12 exhibits reduced in vitro activity with the MERS-CoV NSP8. This asymmetric cross-species compatibility highlights both the evolutionary conservation and virus-specific adaptation of coronavirus polymerase-cofactor interactions. Together, these findings provide a structural and mechanistic framework for understanding MERS-CoV RNA synthesis and establish its conserved RTC as a potential target for the development of broadly acting coronavirus antivirals.

items.title: Auditing frozen chemical language model embeddings for drug-delivery screening: fingerprint baselines, random-initialization controls, and scaffold-memorization control tasks
items.abstract_or_text: Frozen embeddings from pretrained chemical language models (cLMs) are widely used as features for ADMET and drug-delivery prediction, often with a linear probe and little validation of what the representation actually contributes. We audit two small public cLMs (ChemBERTa-77M-MLM and ChemBERTa-77M-MTR, 3.4M parameters each) on three delivery-relevant endpoints from openly licensed sources: blood–brain barrier penetration (B3DB, CC0), PAMPA permeability (NCATS via PubChem), and Caco-2 permeability (OpenADMET, CC-BY-4.0). For each endpoint we compare frozen mean-pooled embeddings with (i) Morgan-fingerprint linear probes with train-only tuned regularization, (ii) the same architecture with random weights (five initialization seeds), and (iii) scaffoldconstant control tasks in the style of Hewitt and Liang that quantify how much a linear probe can score by memorizing scaffold identity. On observed means, tuned fingerprint probes are slightly ahead of frozen embeddings on all three endpoints (paired per-split differences of 0.016–0.032 in AUROC or R2, smaller than split-to-split variation); trained embeddings exceed random-initialization controls by 0.04–0.10; endpoint probes are selective above scaffold-memorization controls, and the memorization ceiling rises with layer depth in the primary MLM model. Decodability of bulk physicochemical descriptors (molecular weight, TPSA, fraction sp3, aromatic rings) is largely preserved under random initialization, indicating an architectural rather than learned origin for those signals; learned increments appear for logP, hydrogen-bond donors, and rotatable bonds. We quantify three practitioner pitfalls: pooling choice changes endpoint AUROC by up to 0.05; tuning the fin- gerprint baseline’s regularization changes it by up to 0.03 AUROC or 0.20 R2; and scaffoldsplit construction details change means by up to 0.04, exceeding seed standard deviations. The source datasets are public and cited; all curation scripts, pipeline code, and per-seed results are included in the accompanying package. The study is compute-bounded to CPU and small models, which limits the generality of the conclusions to that regime.

items.title: Functional-Group Knowledge Is Structured in Language Models Before It Is Spoken
items.abstract_or_text: Language models increasingly serve as the reasoning core of agents for chemistry and materials science, where they must interpret molecular structure before planning syntheses or proposing materials. Yet their outputs show only what they say, not what they know. Given a prompt such as “The primary functional group in 1-Fluorobutane (CCCCF) is”, a small general-purpose model may answer “the alkyne group” instead of an alkyl fluoride. The output alone cannot tell whether the model failed to recognize the fluorine or recognized it and failed to say so. We address this by reading the internal representations of five open-source models (a general-purpose base, three chemistry-trained models, and a reasoning-distilled model) on prompts covering 92 molecules and 20 functional groups. Even without chemistry training, the models organize functional groups by chemical family, and they encode chemical differences as consistent directions. The shift from thioether (R−S−R′) to thiol (R−SH), added to ether (R−O−R′), lands nearest alcohol (R−OH). This structure emerges abruptly in the middle layers, where representations shift from tracking the wording of the prompt to tracking the functional group. The base model names the correct functional group in only 58.5% of prompts, the lowest of the five, yet it encodes functional-group families and preserves chemically meaningful patterns. Its errors are mostly failures to answer rather than wrong answers. Functional-group knowledge is structured in the model before it is spoken. Chemistry fine-tuning acts less by adding this knowledge than by reorganizing it, making functional groups rather than prompt wording dominate the representation. These results suggest that evaluating chemical language models through outputs alone can underestimate the chemical information they encode. Representation analysis can distinguish a lack of knowledge from a failure to express it, which matters when choosing or adapting models for chemical agents.

items.title: Can LLM Agents Improve Imperfect Earth System Model Parameterizations?
items.abstract_or_text: Earth system models (ESMs) rely on parameterizations to represent unresolved processes such as convection, cloud microphysics, and turbulence. However, translating advances in physical understanding into stable, validated parameterizations and integrating them into ESMs often takes years. Agentic AI could accelerate this process and enable more systematic exploration of design choices. Using warm-rain collision-coalescence as a test case, we evaluate agents' ability to synthesize scientific literature, reimplement published bulk parameterizations, and propose new functional forms as differentiable JAX code. We compare conventional parameterizations, data-driven emulators, and agent-generated closures against high-fidelity superdroplet simulations, repeating unattended experiments across ten language models. With expert guidance or iterative feedback, agents produced executable, differentiable, mass-conserving code, although unattended performance depended strongly on the scheme and language model. Iterative feedback lowered median rollout error for eight of ten models. Retuned physical schemes matched or outperformed many learned parameterizations at substantially lower computational cost, but two of 100 unattended agent-generated closures achieved slightly lower rain-mass error than the most accurate retuned scheme on held-out simulations.

items.title: DistDebug-Bench: Can LLM Agents Diagnose Bugs in Distributed Systems?
items.abstract_or_text: LLM agents show strong potential in software engineering tasks such as competitive programming and code synthesis. Existing benchmarks, however, largely focus on small-scale settings such as self-contained Python modules, leaving distributed systems, an essential class of production software, under-examined. We introduce DistDebug-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating agents' ability to diagnose complex-system failures at the code level. It curates 120 high-quality real-world bugs from 11 widely used distributed systems, spanning 5 programming languages and 10 failure patterns. Through an extensive evaluation of state-of-the-art LLMs and agents, we identify substantial gaps between current agents and real-world debugging tasks. A recurring gap is tunnel vision due to a lack of explicit reasoning structure and nondeterminism from inconsistent tool-use scope. The benchmark and evaluator are available at https://github.com/OrderLab/distdebug-bench, with agent traces and a leaderboard at https://distdebug.com.

items.title: PaddleMaterials: An End-to-End Deep Learning Toolkit for Materials Science
items.abstract_or_text: Machine learning supports materials design, atomistic simulation and experimental characterization, yet models and workflows remain fragmented. We present PaddleMaterials, an open-source framework integrating heterogeneous materials-learning tasks while preserving task-specific representations and scientific semantics. It unifies data processing, training, evaluation, pretrained-model management and workflows across six task classes: property prediction, structure generation, machine-learning interatomic potentials, electronic-structure fields, spectrum elucidation and microscopy image processing. Task interfaces record physical quantities, units, aggregation conventions and references, making cross-task composition verifiable. A shared compiler backend enables switching from dynamic-graph to compiled execution through one setting, using graph optimization, operator fusion and hardware-targeted code generation without changing model definitions. Across 65 model instances in 11 groups, compiled execution accelerated every instance in eight groups, with group median speedups of 11%-224% and group maximum speedups of 11%-336%. Case studies on LiMnO2 and toluene link structure generation or spectrum elucidation, interatomic-potential relaxation, property prediction and electron-density prediction, using same-geometry density functional theory (DFT) calculations as references. For LiMnO2, predicted formation energies for generated and relaxed structures differed from same-geometry PBE+U references by at most 7 meV per atom, while the computational cost of model steps was less than one-twentieth of a DFT single-point calculation. PaddleMaterials extends unified materials workflows beyond conventional property, potential and structure-generation tasks while supporting verifiable cross-task operations and compiled execution.

items.title: LUCA: A Synthetic World for Experimental Reasoning
items.abstract_or_text: An experimental agent can succeed for the wrong reasons. Evaluations, however, often focus on the outcome, not the experiments, evidence, and inferences that produced it. We introduce LUCA, a configurable synthetic world for evaluating this process under fully known ground truth. Agents learn unknown regulatory systems through budgeted experimentation, then predict unseen interventions, diagnose hidden faults, and attempt rescues. This setup allows us to evaluate experiment selection, prediction, diagnosis, and intervention separately. Across seven frontier LLMs and three baselines, these capabilities dissociate sharply. Agents frequently rescue malfunctioning systems while diagnosing the wrong fault; diagnosis varies 7x across models while prediction varies only 1.4x. Models also adopt surprisingly different experimental strategies, and greater exploration does not reliably yield better performance. In one failure mode, agents often perform the experiment needed to distinguish competing causes, but still fail to use the resulting evidence. LUCA turns these hidden failures into measurable behaviours, providing a controlled environment to study where experimental agents succeed and fail. Code: https://github.com/RelationRx/luca.

items.title: Molecular crowding differentially regulates magnetic field-dependent fluorescence, recovery kinetics, and photostability of the magnetosensitive protein MagLOV2
items.abstract_or_text: Macromolecular crowding and solvent composition can alter protein conformation, diffusion, hydration, and cofactor photophysics, yet their influence on magnetically sensitive flavoproteins is poorly understood. We tested seven molecular environments in MagLOV2-overexpressing Escherichia coli lysate using a custom-built, high-intensity magnetofluorescence platform. Five-point concentration series of Dextran 70, Ficoll PM70, PEG6000, PEG3350, glycerol, ethylene glycol, and bovine serum albumin (BSA) were measured at 22 mT under continuous 6.12 W/cm2 blue-light excitation. Dextran 70, Ficoll PM70, and PEG6000 progressively attenuated the negative magnetic field effect (MFE), whereas PEG3350 shifted toward mild enhancement at higher concentrations. Glycerol and ethylene glycol enhanced the negative MFE despite producing the strongest slowing of recovery upon the field being switched off (OFF-recovery), while BSA modestly enhanced MFE and accelerated OFF-recovery. Across 105 treatment cuvettes, the change in MFE was not globally correlated with changes in the OFF-recovery time constant (r = -0.07, p = 0.449). The initial pre-field illumination period revealed a second phenotype: Dextran and Ficoll increased late fluorescence loss, whereas glycerol and BSA were photoprotective. Pre-field fluorescence loss correlated moderately with MFE change across the full dataset (r = 0.474, p = 3.28 x 10-7) but not consistently within crowder classes. These findings show that MagLOV2 spin-dependent magnetofluorescence is shaped by crowder chemistry, polymer size, solvent environment, recovery kinetics, and photostability rather than by a single generic crowding or viscosity mechanism.

items.title: An Audited Open Record of Three Deep-Blue TADF Host Materials with Benchmark Tasks for Machine Learning
items.abstract_or_text: We present an audited measurement record of three phosphine-oxide hosts for deep-blue thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF), with provenance metadata and benchmark tasks for machine learning. A scripted audit converted a 5276-file archive into 1662 files (1639 instrument files and 23 instrument-side fit tables) in ten record families, identifying 44 files stored under incorrect material or medium labels and retaining parsed settings, provenance tiers and quality flags. Colour recomputed from the spectra agrees with instrument reports, while gradient-boosted trees detect Raman-scattering artefacts in single emission spectra with a grouped ROC AUC of 0.92. Within-host interpolation is feasible, but three materials do not support broad property prediction for unseen hosts; the released scripts, manifest and task tables provide a reproducible baseline and a schema for adding materials.

items.title: MedPsy: State-of-the-Art Small Medical Language Models for Efficient Edge Deployment
items.abstract_or_text: Medical language models promise expert clinical support, but the strongest open-source LLMs remain too large for private edge-device deployment, while compact medical models still trail substantially on knowledge-intensive and real-world healthcare tasks. Reasoning models that fit edge memory budgets can produce long reasoning traces, increasing sequential decoding, end-to-end latency, energy consumption, and KV-cache memory pressure. We present MedPsy, a family of text-only 1.7B and 4B medical language models designed for edge deployment, targeting this accuracy-generation-efficiency trade-off. Our recipe combines a synthetic medical data pipeline over biology, medicine, and health seeds with chain-of-thought targets from a 235B medical-focused LLM teacher; a four-stage post-training curriculum comprising two SFT stages followed by two RL stages with hard-sample mining; and an edge deployment evaluation spanning multiple GGUF quantization variants and real-device inference on laptop and smartphone hardware. On seven closed-ended medical benchmarks, MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-1.5-4B by 19.34 points and matches MedGemma-27B while being 6.75x smaller; MedPsy-1.7B outperforms MedGemma-1.5-4B by 11.42 points despite being less than half its size. On HealthBench-Hard, MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-27B by 15.33 points, while MedPsy-1.7B surpasses it by 11.66 points despite being ~16x smaller. Beyond accuracy, MedPsy reduces average response length by 1.7x (1.7B) and 3.2x (4B) versus its Qwen3 backbones, while Q4_K_M quantization preserves the aggregate score within 1 point of BF16 with ~69% lower disk footprint. In real-device inference, MedPsy-4B's shorter generations translate into 75% lower median end-to-end latency and estimated energy per answer than its Qwen3 backbone at matched quantization, while peak RAM remains below 5 GB across our tested laptop and smartphone configurations.

items.title: Can Agentic AI Undermine Its Own Assurance Loop? Closed-Loop Dependency Assurance for Cognitive Network Digital Twins
items.abstract_or_text: Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Network Digital Twins (NDTs) are increasingly combined to form Cognitive Digital Twins (CDTs) that translate operational intents into network changes and support closed-loop management. However, a network change may achieve its intended objective while disrupting the monitoring or recovery mechanisms needed for subsequent decisions. For example, a service may be rerouted while its latency-monitoring traffic continues along the original path, producing measurements that no longer reflect the service's performance. We propose Closed-Loop Dependency Assurance (CLDA), an assurance mechanism that augments agentic AI-enabled NDTs with dependency-aware validation. In our framework, an agentic AI planner generates and refines network plans, while the NDT evaluates the projected network outcomes of these plans. CLDA extends this analysis using a Loop Dependency Graph (LDG) that connects service requirements to monitoring mechanisms, forwarding paths, failure domains, and recovery prerequisites. CLDA projects candidate actions onto these dependencies, checks intermediate states of multistep plans, and supports deterministic make-before-break repairs using temporary monitoring mechanisms. Unlike the Large Language Model (LLM)-based planner, CLDA uses explicit, deterministic rules for assurance decisions and repair. We evaluate CLDA through controlled reconfigurations, a 240-trial LLM-based planning campaign, and live network execution. A separate synthetic study examines deterministic assurance scalability across network models representing up to 1,024 routers.

items.title: Auto-Research Agent on MSA Organization to Improve Protein-Protein Complex Structure Prediction
items.abstract_or_text: Protein-complex structure prediction with AlphaFold 3 depends on MSA content, depth, and cross-chain pairing. Current pipelines apply uniform recipes, typically maximizing depth and pairing by species, yet even whether cross-chain pairing helps AF3 remains contested. We show that the value of both depth and pairing is strongly target-dependent, so no single recipe is optimal across interfaces. We introduce an autonomous agent that treats a frozen AF3 as a black-box experimental instrument. For each target, the agent formulates biological hypotheses, analyzes and reorganizes the MSA, and iteratively refines sequence selection and pairing using predictor label-free signals alone. On 1{,}015 protein--protein interfaces from three benchmarks released after AF3's training cutoff, the agent improves overall interface DockQ over AF3's default pipeline and fixed MSA recipes on every benchmark, while using on average 60\% fewer MSA sequences than the default. Gains are largest for inter-species heteromers, where species-based pairing is unreliable: mean DockQ increases from 0.465 to 0.612 on FoldBench and from 0.482 to 0.562 on HD439. The improvements arise from both sequence construction and pairing policy, including deliberate non-pairing.These results recast MSA design as a target-specific problem and show that an autonomous agent can adapt it at test time through biological reasoning and self-directed, confidence-guided experimentation.

items.title: Accessed, never disclosed: Silent access to protected health information by medical artificial intelligence agents
items.abstract_or_text: Medical artificial intelligence agents should retrieve patient identifiers only when a task requires them, the data-minimization principle behind the HIPAA minimum necessary standard for protected health information (PHI). An agent can retrieve identifiers without revealing them. Such silent access remains invisible to evaluations that inspect only the output. We embedded canaries in synthetic patient records and linked each tool invocation to canary exposure in the final answers across five language models, four boundary levels, and seven attack frames for identifier-free clinical tasks. Three models invoked the PHI tools unnecessarily, whereas Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 did not. Stronger boundaries reduced this access, and the residual access under the strictest policy was confined to frames in which the user overrode the policy or asserted approval. A pre-execution gate given the task-necessity criterion nearly eliminated this access. Output-only evaluation cannot verify minimum-necessary access; boundaries, gates, and access-log audits are required together.

items.title: Diffusion-Based Synthetic Pretraining for Root Segmentation in Rhizotron Images
items.abstract_or_text: Rhizotrons allow root system architecture to be studied non-destructively in soil. However, automated analysis of rhizotron images remains difficult: roots have low contrast against soil, soil particles resemble fine roots, and deep learning models need many manually annotated images that are slow and subjective to produce. Synthetic images could provide paired images and annotations at scale, but rhizotron images are largely absent from the data used to train generative models. We built a pipeline combining Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), ControlNet and inpainting to generate synthetic rhizotron images with paired root masks. We compared training on synthetic data only, real data only, and synthetic pretraining followed by fine-tuning on real images, using three segmentation models: nnU-Net v2, YOLO26 and Mask2Former. Synthetic-only training reached a Dice score of up to 0.60. Synthetic pretraining followed by fine-tuning on the full real training set (two annotated rhizotron images) reached 0.80, and nnU-Net v2 and Mask2Former reached 0.62 with only two annotated image patches containing visible roots. When real annotations were limited, pretraining also improved segmentation of unseen crops, including lettuce, barley, wheat, maize, tomato, cucumber, French bean and field bean. We also introduced a Soft Dice score that compares predictions with probabilistic consensus maps from seven independent annotators, accounting for annotator disagreement. Models matched average human agreement on low-ambiguity patches but remained below it on high-ambiguity patches. In conclusion, diffusion-generated images can complement real annotations and help scale root segmentation, although their effect on downstream root trait measurements still needs to be validated.

items.title: Integrating Generative AI and Data Science into General Chemistry Laboratories
items.abstract_or_text: The emergence of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini is reshaping research, education, and industry. Recent workforce data indicate a widening gap between declining junior-level opportunities and rising demand for senior-level expertise, underscoring the urgent need to adapt undergraduate chemistry curricula to prepare students for an AI-enabled workforce. To address this challenge, we designed a series of Python-based laboratory experiments for General Chemistry that integrate generative AI with instructor guidance to enhance student learning. The modules focus on (1) using AI tools to support conceptual understanding, (2) applying AI-assisted coding for data visualization and analysis, and (3) introducing machine learning workflows to solve real-world chemistry problems. All activities are implemented in Google Colaboratory, a cloud-based programming platform now integrated with Gemini, which helps students, particularly those without prior programming experience, complete coding tasks with step-by-step instructor guidance. We compare student attitudes toward the use of AI and programming at the beginning and end of the semesters, observing a more positive attitude toward AI use and increased confidence in programming. To demonstrate scalability, three PhD graduate students, two of whom had no prior programming background, successfully led the laboratory sessions using these AI-supported materials, confirming that instructors across a wide range of computational skill levels can teach the experiments. This work demonstrates how generative AI can create more prosperous and equitable learning experiences, equipping students with transferable skills essential for research and industry careers, as well as the evolving STEM workforce.

items.title: Reinforcement Learning in High-Energy Physics: A Survey from Accelerator Control to Theory Exploration
items.abstract_or_text: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a machine learning paradigm in which an agent learns a decision-making policy by interacting with an environment, guided by a scalar reward rather than explicit supervision. Supervised and unsupervised learning have become indispensable tools in high-energy physics (HEP), but they learn from fixed datasets, whereas many HEP tasks are closed-loop decisions: the data an algorithm observes depend on its choices, the feedback is sparse or delayed, and the objective is often measured on a real machine or in a stochastic simulation, not by a differentiable model. This survey reviews the application of RL to such tasks: accelerator control and feedback, data quality monitoring, jet grooming, clustering, and representation, charged particle tracking, beyond-the-Standard-Model (BSM) and string model building, detector design, trigger control, analysis, and formal quantum field theory computation. It provides a self-contained introduction to the underlying RL methods, from model-free and model-based to multi-agent, offline, inverse, and bandit approaches, reviews each domain against its traditional methods, and summarizes the head-to-head comparisons. The applications range from policies deployed on real accelerators and evaluated on recorded collision data to exploratory studies in formal theory. RL is most advantageous for repeated tasks with a fast simulator, decisions inside fast control loops, operation under faults and corrupted measurements, physics-based rewards in place of labels, and sequential discrete constructions with a reusable policy, while Bayesian optimization, genetic algorithms, and differentiable methods remain competitive elsewhere. We conclude with the open challenges that recur across domains, including reward design, sim-to-real transfer, safety, the lack of shared benchmarks, and the statistical validity of policy-driven decisions.

items.title: Can Large Language Model Agents Learn by Watching Tutorial Videos?
items.abstract_or_text: Humans continuously acquire knowledge from carefully crafted materials such as books and tutorial videos, carrying that understanding into future tasks. Millions of such instructional videos are uploaded online every day, yet LLM agents remain unable to exploit this ever-expanding wealth of human teaching. Their capabilities are frozen after training, while parameter updates at scale remain prohibitively expensive. This raises the central question: can LLM agents learn from this vast instructional resource without parameter updates? We introduce Tutorial Agentic Learning (TAL), a nonparametric continual-learning paradigm that consolidates tutorial videos into a persistent, structured tutorialbook memory through a two-stage adversarial process that harvests hard, video-grounded questions and uses them to refine the memory. At inference time, TAL retrieves through a Table-of-Contents (TOC) tree, tying retrieval directly to the model's reasoning rather than to embedding similarity. To study this setting, we introduce VidLearn, a multimodal QA benchmark built from 72 chess tutorial videos spanning 12 openings. On VidLearn, TAL outperforms all evaluated baselines and improves monotonically as more videos are consumed, achieving up to 113% and 91% relative gains over the corresponding vanilla MLLMs on the training and test splits, respectively. In actual gameplay, TAL reaches a stronger opening-phase position than its vanilla counterpart in 69% of head-to-head games. Evaluation in a second domain further demonstrates the generality of TAL. Together, these results highlight instructional videos as a scalable resource for parameter-update-free agent continual learning.

items.title: Beyond Synthesis Conditions: Linking In-situ Growth Dynamics to Carbon Nanotube Forest Properties through Multimodal Machine Learning
items.abstract_or_text: Machine learning for chemical vapor deposition (CVD) of carbon nanotubes (CNTs) has largely mapped static synthesis conditions to final properties, implicitly treating these conditions as a complete description of growth. Here, we test this assumption by integrating gas-flow conditions with in-situ time-resolve growth profiles (growth curves) of vertically aligned CNT forests. We introduce an observation-window analysis, in which prediction is evaluated as a function of observation time by providing models with the growth curve only up to progressively later times, to determine not only whether a property can be predicted, but when the necessary information becomes available during synthesis. Clustering of normalized growth curves revealed distinct growth patterns independent of final forest height. The gas conditions alone could predict the initial growth rate but not the growth lifetime and failed to capture the variation in yield (R^2<0). Adding the growth curve improved yield prediction (R^2~0.4-0.5), with the relevant information emerging during the intermediate and later stages of growth rather than at its onset. In contrast, density and G/D ratio, which forest height does not record, showed no consistent improvement. The maximum height and lifetime could be estimated with moderate accuracy midway through the 10-min growth. Permutation feature importance identified water vapor and H_2, both linked to catalyst activity, as the most informative gas variables. These results indicate that variation unexplained by synthesis conditions is not merely noise but reflects an evolving catalyst state, and they establish mid-growth decision points for autonomous synthesis, enabling early termination of unpromising batches and, ultimately, in-batch adjustment of growth conditions.

items.title: Can agents reliably design therapeutic antibodies?
items.abstract_or_text: Recent work has demonstrated agents driving protein design workflows, either through orchestration of specialized tools or direct manipulation of sequences. Yet the fidelity with which agents follow protein design instructions and the factors contributing to their effectiveness remain understudied. We examine agentic antibody design under two settings: when explicit molecular-editing instructions are provided and when agents receive only previously-scored sequences and are prompted to propose improvements. We call the first task-guided and the second black-box design. For the task-guided setting, we curate ten expert-validated affinity-improvement tasks and show that LLM judges closely reproduce programmatic evaluations of instruction following. We then study two augmentations: access to antibody-relevant tools and to previously scored design history. Tools improve instruction following (IF) and sequence space exploration while reducing optimization performance, whereas design history reduces IF but improves optimization performance at the expense of exploration. Finally, we combine taskguided and black-box design within an in silico optimization loop and show that our agentic optimizer performs comparably to an established Bayesian optimization baseline.

items.title: WebHarbor: Docking Real Websites for Evolving GUI Agent Environments
items.abstract_or_text: GUI web agents require realistic and interactive environments that remain stable during both evaluation and training. Live website evaluation suffers from changing content, access restrictions, and limited coverage of authenticated workflows, while existing synthetic environments for training often lack functional depth and visual fidelity. We propose WebHarbor, a suite of 153 executable and dockerized website environments that faithfully reconstruct the visual interfaces, content, and functional workflows of real-world web services under deterministic control. We build WebHarbor through task-driven human-agent collaboration, where environments evolve as new tasks expand their functional scope, coding agents implement the required changes, and human contributors audit visual fidelity, functional correctness, and task validity. The resulting suite comprises 3,518 tasks spanning multi-step and post-authentication workflows, where existing works often fail to cover. Beyond reliable evaluation, WebHarbor provides high-fidelity synthetic web environments for cost-efficient reinforcement learning (RL). We demonstrate that a Qwen 4B-level GUI agent trained with RL in WebHarbor generalizes to unseen tasks and performs competitively with leading open-source GUI web agents across four benchmarks. The code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/aiming-lab/WebHarbor.

items.title: SQLoom: Set-Contrastive Learning of Syntactic, Semantic, and Logical Dependencies for Text-to-SQL
items.abstract_or_text: Text-to-SQL translates natural language questions into SQL queries, enabling database access without writing SQL. Fine-tuning open-weight large language models (LLMs) is cost-effective, but existing methods treat SQL as ordinary text and optimize token-level likelihood without explicitly modeling its syntactic, semantic, and logical requirements. Thus, a single incorrect alias or comparison operator can invalidate a query while contributing little to training loss. We propose SQLoom, a constraint-aware fine-tuning framework with supervision at three levels: syntactic validity under SQL grammar and database schema, semantic alignment between query decisions and the question, and logical consistency across dependent clause decisions. SQLoom extends supervised fine-tuning with a unified set-contrastive objective favoring sets of correct outputs over minimally different incorrect ones at each level. LLM agents propose this supervision, which a SQL parser and execution on counterexample databases verify. We also release Spider-Refined, a training dataset correcting 378 flawed Spider annotations and enriching database schemas. Experiments on Spider, BIRD, and three perturbed Spider variants show that SQLoom improves execution accuracy for Qwen3-1.7B from 62.9% zero-shot to 88.7% on Spider development, reaching 89.2% on Spider test and 73.4% on BIRD development. It outperforms fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and agent-based baselines with up to 70 billion parameters. On question perturbations, SQLoom loses at most 0.6 accuracy points versus up to 12.1 for agent-based methods. It generates SQL in a single pass at 0.42s per query, 23\times faster than a GPT-4-based agent method. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of set-contrastive supervision over token-level training.

items.title: HLSClaw: Bringing Vibe Coding to High-Level Synthesis through Skill-Based Agentic Harness
items.abstract_or_text: LLM agents are rapidly shifting software development toward intent-driven vibe coding, yet their effectiveness drops sharply in high-level synthesis (HLS), where code optimization must jointly consider design structure, directive search, and downstream hardware constraints. Existing HLS optimization approaches, including both heuristic-based methods and recent LLM-assisted pipelines, typically operate at fixed abstraction levels or in weakly coupled stages, limiting their ability to leverage the strong interplay between source code restructuring and directive search outcomes. Our key insight is that HLS optimization can be reframed from a fixed, hardwired transformation pipeline into a skill-based agentic control problem: an LLM agent equipped with modular, executable optimization skills and a feedback-driven orchestrator can autonomously navigate the coupled space of code restructuring and directive search. This motivates the design of HLSClaw, the first HLS-specific, skill-based agentic harness for holistic HLS optimization. On real-world HLS benchmarks, HLSClaw achieves a 39.12x geometric-mean latency speedup, outperforming the compiler baseline ScaleHLS by 1.98x, and surpassing the commercial coding agents Claude Code and Codex by 1.86x and 1.70x, respectively, while maintaining strong timing robustness.

items.title: GPU infrastructure for ML/MM with electrostatic embedding for enzyme chemistry
items.abstract_or_text: We present a fully GPU-native framework for machine learning/molecular mechanics (ML/MM) enhanced sampling simulations with electrostatic embedding, demonstrated on an enzymatic reaction. The framework combines a JAX port of the pretrained MACE-POLAR-1-M model, an electrostatic embedding scheme compatible with the MACE-POLAR architecture, and integration with JAX-MD and PLUMED-JAX for end-to-end compiled enhanced sampling. The implementation is developed using GPT-6.1-Sol within Codex, with reasoning effort set to high. Using replica exchange umbrella sampling, we calculate the free energy profile of nucleophilic substitution in haloalkane dehalogenase in approximately 200 H100 GPU hours, treating the entire protein and reactants with MACE-POLAR-1-M-JAX and most of the solvent with molecular mechanics.

items.title: Design and Benchmarking of CK2α′-Preferring Inhibitors for Huntington’s Disease: The Limits of Structure-Based Isoform Selectivity
items.abstract_or_text: Protein kinase CK2 acts through two catalytic isoforms, CK2α (A1) and CK2α′ (A2), whose ATP-binding sites differ at only two hinge positions, making isoform-selective inhibition difficult. We tested whether a standard structure-based pipeline can design and rank CK2α′-preferring compounds. In a paired benchmark of 140 compounds measured against both isoforms, none of the five docking-derived criteria, computed with GNINA and convolutional neural network rescoring, correlated with measured selectivity (ρ = −0.19 to +0.12), and for matched pairs differing by a single linker methylene, the scoring reversed the experimental order. The only reliable determinant of preference, a two-carbon linker within the benzo[c][2,6]naphthyridine scaffold, was obtained from the measured activities rather than from any computed score. Molecular-dynamics ensembles of the two isoforms overlapped (0.88 Å between versus 0.72–0.96 Å within), placing the selectivity signal below the resolution of the methods. From an enumerated series, EV043 showed the largest end-point free-energy preference for CK2α′ (ΔΔGb -7.74 kcal/mol), although this value remained sensitive to the starting pose in CK2α, while the non-selective inhibitor CX-4945 was reproduced correctly (+0.08 kcal/mol). Distinguishing CK2α′ from CK2α therefore requires alchemical free-energy methods supported by experimental validation.

items.title: vibe-qc: expert-directed agentic engineering for scientific software development
items.abstract_or_text: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can implement scientific software, but useful development also requires executable comparisons, inspectable results and a record of scientific decisions. This case study examines the tooling that enables semi-autonomous electronic-structure software development under expert direction. VIBE-QC supplies molecular and periodic calculations; vibe-scheduler queues and manages calculations across clusters and a fleet of workstations; vibe-viewer and the Quantum Visualization Format (QVF) connect numerical outputs to portable inspection and reproducible figures. Retained development records illustrate how these tools preserve failed attempts, distinguish changes in physical conventions from implementation errors, and separate measured differences from expert-selected acceptance criteria. Publication-specific calculations were run with VIBE-QC 0.18.x and use formaldehyde to connect controlled numerical comparisons with visual inspection; diamond and lithium hydride provide periodic Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) examples with explicit convergence checks. The expert sets the physical problem, selects diagnostic controls and interprets the evidence; AI agents implement and execute those tasks. The resulting account identifies practical requirements for sustained AI-assisted scientific development. It establishes a traceable process within one project, without claiming autonomous scientific judgment or a measured productivity advantage.

items.title: DeliverBench: Benchmarking AI Agents on Delivering Realistic Multi-Stage Professional Projects
items.abstract_or_text: LLM agents are judged by what they deliver, and in professional work what gets delivered is a project, not a task. A project pays off only if the whole package holds, and one weak part can limit the value of the rest. Yet existing benchmarks mostly test agents on one task at a time, leaving a gap between the capability we measure and the outcome that makes agents useful. To address this gap, we introduce DeliverBench, which tests whether agents can carry a project from brief to final delivery. Its 11 projects, spanning financial due diligence, legal contract drafting, and drug safety reporting, are reconstructed with 13 domain experts from real materials and chain 150 subtasks through 2-15 rounds of new materials and client feedback. Because no reference outputs are injected, agents inherit their own errors from one task to the next. Expert rubrics then score every checkpoint as well as the final package. Across seven model-harness systems, even the best system scores only 65.0 out of 100 on final delivery and passes 50.0% of subtasks at a 90-point threshold. The failures are often failures of carrying work forward: in one audit project, all seven systems addressed the review findings, but only one preserved traceability. Together, these results suggest that task-level capability does not simply compose into delivery, which also depends on keeping the work coherent as it evolves.

items.title: A Common Language for Dynamic Graphs: Interaction Tokenization Enables Foundation Models
items.abstract_or_text: Dynamic graphs capture evolving interactions in Web systems, including online communication, user engagement, and recommendation. Graph foundation models aim to reuse predictive capabilities across networks, but extending this capability to dynamic graphs faces two challenges. First, node identities are graph-specific, and similar interaction patterns can appear at different temporal and activity scales, making histories difficult to represent consistently across networks. Second, the predictive roles of historical patterns vary across interaction dynamics, limiting transfer from a narrow range of training processes. In this paper, we show that a common interaction language, combined with learning across diverse interaction processes, offers a basis for dynamic graph foundation modeling. We propose CL-DGFM, a Common Language Dynamic Graph Foundation Model for temporal link prediction. Its Dynamic Interaction Tokenizer encodes interaction memory, historical connectivity, and ordered destination transitions into calibrated tabular inputs, making dynamic histories accessible to existing predictors without an additional trainable graph encoder. Its Dynamic Interaction Prior trains a pretrained tabular foundation predictor across diverse synthetic dynamics. Labeled historical context guides prediction, with a Contextual Value Adapter modulating attention values. The model transfers to real graphs without target-graph parameter updates. Experiments on TGB and TGB-Seq demonstrate competitive performance. Further comparisons show that the common language supports basic machine learning and neural models, and enables direct use of frozen tabular foundation models on dynamic graphs.

items.title: Human-Supervised Artificial Intelligence Researchers in Electric Power Systems: Knowledge, Physics, Simulation, and Governance for Large Language Models
items.abstract_or_text: Conclusions in power-system research require a clear evidential basis. Researchers need to understand the data sources, modelling assumptions, and solution procedures to assess the conditions under which a conclusion holds. Large language models (LLMs) can help researchers extract information from documents and translate research requests into code and tool calls, but their outputs still require physical validation. Focusing on human-supervised artificial intelligence (AI) researchers, this review examines power-system LLM applications and related scientific workflows, together with physics-grounded power AI studies, to discuss the conditions for using LLMs in scientific research. In the proposed knowledge-physics-simulation-governance framework, LLMs translate information and coordinate tasks, simulators and validation tools test models, and experts retain authority over critical assumptions, safety boundaries, and final conclusions. Research processes should preserve materials for review so that claims can be traced to their sources, computations can be reproduced, and failed attempts and approvals can be examined. On this basis, a staged development roadmap and requirements for research reporting are proposed. Evaluation should focus on research artifacts and their validation to assess whether LLMs can improve the efficiency of power-system research within clearly defined permissions.

items.title: CHORUS: A proteome-scale atlas of membrane protein interaction interfaces predicted from sequence
items.abstract_or_text: Membrane protein interactions underpin essential cellular processes, yet the residues mediating these interactions remain difficult to identify at scale due to the paucity of experimentally resolved protein complexes within hydrophobic bilayers. Here, we present CHORUS, a sequence-only framework for predicting interaction interfaces in membrane proteins without requiring structural coordinates, multiple sequence alignments, or known interacting partners. By synthesizing complementary latent representations from three protein language models, CHORUS outperforms 18 established sequence- and structure-based methods by a chain-macro average precision value of 0.643 versus 0.613 for ScanNet-MSA on an independent, homology-restricted test set of 4,655 protein chain contexts, with a particularly pronounced advantage within the membrane-embedded interior (0.746 versus 0.645). Using six mammalian mitochondrial respiratory supercomplexes with >100 independent chains, we show that CHORUS-identified intersubunit interaction interfaces accurately delineate the boundaries between buried protein-protein contact surfaces and surrounding lipid-facing regions in complex molecular systems (0.945-0.984). We subsequently applied CHORUS at proteome scale to chart a global landscape of membrane-protein interaction interfaces for 80,619 expert-reviewed membrane protein entries, 70,247 unique sequences, 4,918 species, and 33.7 million residues across the tree of life. The resulting open-access CHORUS Atlas (https://chorus.atlas.sunnylab.org) provides predicted residue interactions across the membrane proteome. Together, CHORUS establishes a sequence-based foundation for systematic investigation of membrane protein assembly and function, potentially facilitating interactome-scale knowledge discovery and allosteric therapeutic design.

items.title: In vivo discovery of blood-brain barrier opening small molecules with FishNAP
items.abstract_or_text: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) maintains neural homeostasis by tightly regulating molecular exchange between the circulation and the brain, but it also restricts drug delivery and thereby limits treatment of neurological disorders. Pharmacological agents that transiently and safely increase BBB permeability could therefore improve brain drug delivery, yet their systematic discovery has been constrained by the limitations of existing approaches. Here we present FishNAP, a non-invasive, high-throughput zebrafish platform for real-time in vivo assessment of BBB permeability. Screening 2,320 FDA-approved small molecules identified seven that increased BBB permeability in zebrafish, with barrier integrity recovering within 24 hours in each case, indicating reversible modulation. Three of these compounds, Calcitriol, Lovastatin and Sunitinib, which act through distinct signaling pathways, also increased BBB permeability in adult mice through both tight junction disruption and increased transcytosis. FishNAP thus enables the identification of conserved modulators of BBB function with translational potential for brain drug delivery.

items.title: Incorporating Polarization into ML/MM Endpoint Calculations for Protein–Ligand Affinity Ranking
items.abstract_or_text: Endpoint free-energy calculations combine low computational cost with reasonable accuracy and are widely used to rank protein–ligand affinities, yet describing charge polarization in these calculations remains a challenge. Here we introduce a machine learning/molecular mechanics (ML/MM) framework that incorporates polarizationcorrected mechanical embedding (PCME) and electrostatic embedding (EE) into endpoint calculations, using binding-state-and conformation-dependent ML charges in both the gas-phase energy and polar solvation terms. On a benchmark of 15 targets from the JACS and Merck sets, the PCME and EE routes of ML/MM-PBSA rank affinities better than classical MM-PBSA, raising the median Spearman ρ from 0.216 to 0.343 and 0.329, respectively, at an acceptable computational cost. A charge-source control and the analysis of a representative PTP1B complex show how conformationdependent ML charges resolve asymmetric local electrostatic environments and contribute to the improved ranking of ML/MM-PBSA(PCME) over MM-PBSA. By incorporating charge redistribution into both interaction and solvation energies, this work provides a practical ML/MM endpoint framework for protein–ligand affinity ranking and analysis of the underlying electrostatic contributions.

items.title: Microbial Pyrolysis for the Sustainable Synthesis of Nanoparticle-Embedded Carbon Electrocatalysts
items.abstract_or_text: Electrocatalytic processes are essential for a sustainable global economy, yet conventional catalyst synthesis often relies on hazardous reagents and insulating binders that impede performance. Here, microbial extracellular electron transfer for nanoparticle synthesis is integrated with the controlled pyrolysis of microbial monolayers to generate nanoparticle-embedded carbon electrodes. Surface immobilization of Shewanella oneidensis using DNA "Velcro" yields uniform single-microbe-thick layers that are readily patterned and converted into conductive, turbostratic carbon films at temperatures between 800 °C and 1,100 °C. These bio-derived films exhibit progressive graphitic ordering and reach a minimum sheet resistance of 1.49 kΩ/sq, approaching the performance of pyrolyzed synthetic photoresists. Moreover, by leveraging the intrinsic biosynthetic capabilities of S. oneidensis, 3-5 nm palladium nanoparticles are formed directly on the cell surface and seamlessly integrated into the carbon matrix upon pyrolysis. These composites reduce the hydrogen evolution reaction overpotential by 100 mV. This bottom-up bioengineering approach is anticipated to enable the sustainable, programmable fabrication of next-generation electrocatalysts for diverse energy conversion applications.
